strengths: Generalizes the recent Denoising Score Distillation idea to a much broader class of linear corruption operators (blur, masking, downsampling, Fourier-domain subsampling), unifying it with existing corruption-aware pretraining objectives (Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, Fourier-space Ambient Diffusion) into a single two-phase (pretrain + one-step distillation) framework.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning both natural images (CelebA-HQ, multiple corruption types and noise levels) and a real scientific imaging application (multi-coil FastMRI reconstruction at several acceleration rates), consistently showing that the distilled one-step model outperforms its own teacher diffusion model and other baselines (EM-Diffusion, L1-EDM).

The framework is shown to be directly compatible with publicly released pretrained checkpoints (Ambient Diffusion, Fourier-space Ambient Diffusion), demonstrating practical plug-and-play flexibility without requiring re-pretraining.

A theoretical analysis in a linear low-rank Gaussian data model derives closed-form characterization of the global minimizers of the distillation loss and a Wasserstein-2 bound, giving an interpretable account of why/how the distilled model recovers the clean covariance eigenspace, framing distillation as an implicit regularizer rather than merely an acceleration trick.
Introduces a practical and useful "proximal FID" metric for model/checkpoint selection when no clean validation data is available, validated empirically to closely track true FID.
Reports substantial inference speedups (~25x) and demonstrates strong data efficiency of the distillation phase relative to full pretraining, which is practically valuable.
Extensive appendix with proofs, algorithmic pseudocode for every pretraining/distillation variant, and qualitative sample grids across tasks aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core algorithmic machinery (SiD-based Fisher-divergence distillation, Ambient Tweedie/Ambient Diffusion/Fourier-space objectives) is taken directly from prior work; the main contribution is combining/applying these known components to a wider set of corruption types rather than a fundamentally new method.

No ablation isolating how much of the FID improvement over the teacher is simply the well-known effect of score distillation itself (as in DSD) versus a specific benefit attributable to the paper's proposed extension to blur/inpainting/super-resolution objectives; a baseline distilling from a teacher trained with vanilla (non corruption-aware) objectives under identical settings would help disentangle this.

The theoretical analysis relies on a highly simplified linear/low-rank Gaussian model with a rank-1 closed-form case and an unrealistic "perfect score estimation" assumption (Assumption 2); its connection to the behavior of actual deep, nonlinear diffusion models used in the experiments is only qualitative/heuristic.

Natural-image experiments are limited to a single, relatively low-resolution dataset (CelebA-HQ 64×64); no results on more diverse or higher-resolution benchmarks (e.g., FFHQ, ImageNet) to test generality and scalability of the claims.

Evaluation relies solely on FID; no complementary metrics (precision/recall, diversity, perceptual quality, or human evaluation) or reported variance/multiple-seed results to support the significance of the reported gains.

The method is restricted to unconditional generative modeling from corrupted data and explicitly does not solve conditional inverse problems (acknowledged as a limitation), which somewhat limits the direct practical utility highlighted by the medical-imaging motivation.

All tested corruptions are linear (blur, masking, downsampling, Fourier subsampling); the more complex/nonlinear corruption scenarios mentioned as motivation in the introduction (e.g., nonlinear distortions) are not empirically evaluated.

Some overclaiming in framing (e.g., "first distillation framework capable of addressing general inverse problems in an unsupervised setting") given closely related concurrent works (EM-Diffusion, DSD) already target similar corrupted-data generative learning settings.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., inconsistent notation/typos such as "Muti-Coil", some garbled symbols in equations) suggest limited proofreading.

strengths: The paper extends Denoising Score Distillation (DSD) from the pure-noise setting to a broader class of linear corruption operators (blur, masking/inpainting, downsampling, Fourier-domain masking), and shows the framework can be plugged into several existing corruption-aware pretraining losses (Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, Fourier-Space Ambient Diffusion), giving a reasonably unified two-phase recipe.

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 1) generalizes the DSD linear-model analysis to general linear measurement operators A, characterizing the global minimizers of the distillation loss and showing the solution recovers a noise-dependent scaling of the clean eigenspace plus a kernel component, with an explicit Wasserstein-2 bound; the proof is carried out in detail in the appendix.

Empirical results consistently show the one-step distilled model improving over its own teacher diffusion model (trained purely on corrupted data) in FID across several corruption types and severities, and also compare favorably against EM-Diffusion (which additionally uses 50 clean images) and L1-EDM in the multi-coil MRI setting.
The proposed 'proximal FID' offers a practical, clean-data-free model selection heuristic that could be useful more broadly in the corrupted-data generative modeling literature.

The method is demonstrated to be compatible with publicly released Ambient Diffusion / Fourier-Space Ambient Diffusion checkpoints, showing some practical flexibility, and the distillation yields a large (~20x) inference speedup over the multi-step teacher.
Implementation and algorithmic details (Algorithms 1-6, hyperparameters, training compute) are documented fairly thoroughly, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination of existing building blocks: DSD/SiD-style score distillation plus pre-existing corruption-aware pretraining objectives (Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, Fourier-Space Ambient Diffusion) from prior papers; the 'generalization' is conceptually straightforward (swap the pretraining loss, keep the same distillation recipe), which limits the degree of novelty for a top-tier venue.

All natural-image experiments are conducted at a very low resolution (64x64 CelebA-HQ), with no demonstration at higher, more practically relevant resolutions; this substantially limits the significance of the empirical claims relative to modern generative modeling standards.

The theoretical result is restricted to an idealized linear/low-rank Gaussian data model with perfectly known score functions and (for tractability) a rank-1 generator; it is unclear how much insight this toy analysis provides about the behavior of deep, nonlinear U-Net-based diffusion models used in the actual experiments.

Baselines are narrow: the main comparison is against the paper's own teacher model (which score distillation is already known to improve upon, per DSD) and a single few-shot baseline (EM-Diffusion) or a single compressed-sensing baseline (L1-EDM); no comparison is made to clean-data-trained diffusion models to contextualize the remaining quality gap, nor to alternative distillation objectives (e.g., KL-based SDS/DMD) despite the paper's claim of compatibility with various divergences.

The noisy random-inpainting setting is reported to be unstable when combining Ambient Diffusion's inpainting loss with Tweedie correction, and the authors sidestep this rather than resolving it, suggesting the framework's 'flexible integration' claim is not fully realized in practice.

Qualitative figures are low-resolution thumbnail grids that are difficult to visually assess; several generated samples (e.g., deblurring, random inpainting at high corruption) still look noticeably degraded/blurry, raising questions about the real-world visual quality gain beyond the FID metric.

Despite emphasizing 'high distillation data efficiency,' the overall pipeline still requires an expensive teacher pretraining phase (up to 100M iterations per EDM protocol) before distillation, so total compute cost is substantial and not clearly cheaper than alternative approaches.

The paper's scope for 'scientific imaging' generalization rests on a single modality/dataset (FastMRI), limiting evidence for the claimed broad applicability to scientific domains mentioned in the introduction (astronomy, seismology, etc.).

strengths: Extends Denoising Score Distillation (DSD) to a broader and more practically relevant class of corruptions (blurring, inpainting, super-resolution, Fourier-domain masking), unifying score distillation with existing corruption-aware pretraining objectives (Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, Fourier-space Ambient Diffusion).

Provides a theoretical analysis in a tractable linear low-rank Gaussian model that characterizes the global minimizers of the distillation objective and shows recovery of the clean covariance eigenspace up to a controlled Wasserstein-2 error, offering a principled explanation for why distillation acts as an implicit regularizer/denoiser rather than only an acceleration technique.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across both natural images (CelebA-HQ, multiple corruption types and noise levels) and a real scientific imaging application (multi-coil FastMRI), with consistent improvements of the one-step distilled student over its corrupted teacher and over baselines such as EM-Diffusion in most settings.

Demonstrates practical flexibility by directly distilling from existing third-party pretrained checkpoints (Ambient Diffusion, Fourier-Space Ambient Diffusion) rather than only from self-trained teachers, which strengthens claims of generality.

Proposes a proximal FID metric for model/checkpoint selection when clean reference data is unavailable, addressing a genuine practical gap in fully unsupervised training pipelines, and shows it tracks true FID reasonably closely.

Reports large inference speedups (about 25x) from one-step generation versus multi-step teacher sampling, and shows the distillation process is comparatively data/iteration efficient relative to full diffusion pretraining.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to a single natural-image dataset at low resolution (CelebA-HQ 64x64) plus one MRI dataset; no results on more complex/higher-resolution datasets (e.g., ImageNet, FFHQ-256+) or additional corruption operators (e.g., nonlinear degradations, real noise), which limits evidence for the generality claimed in the abstract/intro.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat narrow: EM-Diffusion is compared only in the few-shot (50 clean images) regime and RSD underperforms it in the noisy Gaussian-deblurring case, which is glossed over; there is limited comparison to other recent one-step/score-distillation baselines (e.g., DMD, SiD variants applied naively without corruption-awareness) to isolate the source of gains (distillation vs. corruption-aware pretraining vs. both).

The theoretical analysis relies on a fairly restrictive linear, rank-1/low-rank Gaussian generative model and a linear generator parameterization; it is unclear how much insight this provides into the actual nonlinear U-Net-based diffusion models used in experiments, and no empirical verification of the linear theory's predictions (e.g., checking eigenspace recovery in a controlled synthetic experiment) is provided.

The method still requires knowledge of (or the ability to sample/replicate) the corruption operator A and noise level sigma for both pretraining and the re-corruption step during distillation (Algorithm 6, lines 13/17); despite the claim in Appendix B that the exact operator need not be known, the paper does not clearly demonstrate robustness to a misspecified or only approximately known corruption operator.

Distillation introduces an additional training phase with its own instability risks (paper notes divergence requiring early stopping, and instability of certain losses in noisy inpainting settings), but there is limited quantitative characterization of training stability, sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., the SiD balancing parameter alpha), or variance across runs/seeds.

Some quantitative results are somewhat mixed or marginal (e.g., RSD only modestly better or worse than baselines in some noisy settings such as Gaussian deblurring at sigma=0.2 vs EM-Diffusion, R=2 MRI vs L1-EDM only slightly better), and statistical significance (multiple seeds, confidence intervals) is not reported for any table.

Clarity issues: some notation is dense/overloaded (e.g., reuse of tilde-M, A appearing both as generic operator and in the MRI section with a different meaning), and the paper defers many core distillation and algorithmic details to lengthy appendices, making the main text somewhat hard to fully assess in isolation.

strengths: Proposes a unified two-phase framework (corruption-aware pretraining + measurement-respecting score distillation) that cleanly subsumes denoising, blur, random inpainting, super-resolution, and Fourier-space MRI reconstruction as special cases, with a single algorithmic template (Alg. 1).

Extensive empirical evaluation across CIFAR-10, FFHQ, CelebA-HQ, AFHQ-v2, and multi-coil FastMRI, under both noiseless and noisy regimes, consistently showing the distilled one-step generator surpasses its corruption-aware diffusion teacher and outperforms zero-/few-shot baselines (Ambient Diffusion, EM-Diffusion, SFBD, L1-EDM) without any clean images.

Interesting and somewhat counter-intuitive empirical finding that score distillation can substantially improve sample quality beyond mere acceleration when training data is corrupted, with a plausible mode-seeking-vs-mode-covering explanation and supporting FID/Recall statistics.

Provides theoretical analysis in a linear/Gaussian setting (Theorems 1-4) characterizing global minimizers of the distillation objective and quantifying Wasserstein-distance improvement over the noisy teacher, plus a more general (though assumption-heavy) Fisher-divergence bound (Theorem 5) connecting distillation loss to measurement-space and image-space distributional closeness.
Introduces Proximal FID, a practical model-selection heuristic for the clean-data-unavailable setting, and shows it tracks true FID closely across multiple datasets/operators.

Reasonably thorough ablations: distillation-loss choice, training data size, unknown/misspecified noise level, mixed noise levels, and downstream conditional inverse-problem usage, plus detailed appendix algorithms/hyperparameters supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the corruption-aware diffusion objectives (Table 1) and the distillation loss (SiD) are both taken directly from prior work; the main new ingredient is applying the same corruption pipeline to generator outputs during distillation, which is a relatively small algorithmic delta over existing pipelines.

The general theoretical guarantees (Section F.3) rest on strong, essentially results-assuming conditions (near-optimality Assumption 6, Poincaré-type Assumption 5, and a 'measurement injectivity' condition for image-space transfer) that are least likely to hold precisely for the non-invertible operators (masking, blur, subsampling) that are the paper's central motivating examples, creating a gap between the theory's scope (denoising/near-injective settings) and the breadth of empirical claims.

Experiments are limited to low/moderate resolutions (32x32 CIFAR-10, 64x64 face/animal datasets); no evidence at higher resolution or more complex/diverse image distributions, which limits confidence that the 'high-fidelity' claims generalize to more realistic generative-modeling settings.

Ablation of distillation losses (Table 18) shows SDS/DMD performing extremely poorly (FID > 200) using un-tuned default hyperparameters, while SiD is favored; this makes the 'choice of distillation loss' comparison and the generality of the 'distillation beyond acceleration' claim less convincing, since the effect may be partly an artifact of hyperparameter mismatch rather than an intrinsic property of distillation.

Fairness of compute/budget comparisons across baselines (EM-Diffusion, SFBD, Ambient Diffusion) is not fully controlled for; total compute (Phase I + Phase II) versus baseline training budgets is not explicitly equalized, making some FID improvements harder to attribute purely to the proposed method.

MRI evaluation relies solely on FID against corrupted training data without any PSNR/SSIM validation against available ground-truth references (e.g., using held-out fully-sampled MRI slices), which would strengthen the clinical relevance of the claimed 'real-world applicability'.

Minor presentation issues: some references appear duplicated/possibly tangential to the paper's core topic (e.g., citations to text-to-image editing benchmarking), and dense/lengthy appendix theory sections could be better connected back to the specific experimental settings they are meant to support.

strengths: Proposes a unified two-phase pipeline (corruption-aware diffusion pretraining + score distillation with re-corruption of generated samples) that spans a wide range of degradation types: additive noise, Gaussian blur, random inpainting, super-resolution, and Fourier-space multi-coil MRI undersampling, all learned without any clean data.

Extensive empirical evaluation across CIFAR-10, FFHQ, CelebA-HQ, AFHQ-v2 and real multi-coil FastMRI data, consistently showing FID improvements of the distilled one-step generator over its corruption-aware diffusion teacher and over relevant few-shot/zero-shot baselines (EM-Diffusion, SFBD, TweedieDiff, Ambient Diffusion variants).

The central empirical/conceptual claim -- that score distillation under corrupted-data training yields substantially larger quality gains than under clean-data training, attributed to the mode-seeking behavior of the reverse-divergence distillation objective -- is a potentially useful observation for the field and is supported qualitatively (2D toy example, Precision/Recall numbers) as well as by a dedicated theoretical section.

Introduces 'Proximal FID', a practical model-selection heuristic that substitutes clean-reference FID with FID computed after re-corrupting generated samples, addressing a genuine gap (prior corrupted-data papers do not specify how to perform model selection without clean validation data); empirically shown to track true FID closely in several settings.

Fairly extensive ablations: data-scale sensitivity, choice of distillation loss (SDS/DMD/SiD), robustness to misspecified/unknown noise level, and heterogeneous per-sample noise, plus reasonable implementation/reproducibility details in the appendix (hyperparameters, algorithms for each pretraining variant).

Includes a rigorous (if stylized) theoretical analysis in a linear-Gaussian/low-rank setting with full proofs (Theorems 1-4) and a more general, if looser, Fisher-divergence-based guarantee (Theorem 5) attempting to explain when distillation improves over the noisy/corrupted teacher.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the two core building blocks (corruption-aware diffusion training methods such as Ambient Diffusion/Ambient Tweedie/Fourier-space Ambient Diffusion, and SiD-style score distillation) are both taken directly from prior work; the paper's main new ingredient is re-applying the same corruption operator to generator outputs during distillation (Algorithm 1, line 6), which is a relatively simple architectural choice rather than a fundamentally new method.

The theoretical results that most directly support the headline claim are derived under strong, unrealistic assumptions (Gaussian/low-rank data, linear low-rank generator, perfect score estimation, and for the more general Theorem 5, several unverifiable error terms like Δ(θ̂), ε_φ, λ0). The bounds are not empirically estimated/validated against the deep-network experiments, so the connection between theory and the reported CIFAR/FFHQ/CelebA-HQ results remains largely qualitative/intuitive rather than quantitatively verified.

All main experiments are restricted to small/low-resolution datasets (32x32 CIFAR-10, 64x64 FFHQ/CelebA-HQ/AFHQ-v2) and small-matrix MRI reconstruction; there is no evidence the approach scales to higher-resolution or more complex/diverse data (e.g., ImageNet-scale or text-conditional generation), which limits the generality of the 'high-fidelity' claims made in the abstract/title.

FID is the primary (often sole) metric reported for most tables; broader metrics (Precision/Recall/KID/IS) are only reported for CIFAR-10 in the appendix, leaving the quality claims on FFHQ/CelebA-HQ/AFHQ-v2/MRI largely dependent on a single, known-to-be-imperfect metric, especially for small-sample/low-resolution regimes.

Proximal FID's validity as a model-selection proxy is only checked on the same datasets/settings used for the main results (a form of circularity); there is no test of whether it remains reliable under distribution shift, novel corruption types, or adversarial/non-ideal generator behavior, so its practical reliability as a general-purpose tool is not fully established.

The downstream conditional inverse-problem experiments (Sec. 4.7/ Appendix D.3) are limited in scope (single dataset, small number of baselines/test images, one specific operator), making this part of the contribution feel preliminary rather than a fully validated application.

Some reported gains are modest or data/task-dependent (e.g., MRI R=2 acceleration improvement over L1-EDM is comparatively small, and qualitative MRI reconstructions in Fig. 3 are difficult to visually differentiate from baselines), suggesting the practical significance of the method may vary substantially by regime despite the paper's broad framing of consistent improvement.

The explanation for why distillation helps more under corruption (reverse-KL/Fisher divergence mode-seeking) is a known general property of distillation objectives (already observed to help even with clean data in cited prior work); the paper's incremental claim is mainly that this effect is 'amplified' under corruption, but a more controlled experiment isolating corruption severity vs. distillation gain (holding architecture/compute fixed) is not clearly provided to rigorously establish this amplification claim beyond aggregate benchmark comparisons.

strengths: Unifying framework: RSD generalizes score distillation to a broad class of corruption operators (identity/denoising, blur, masking, subsampling, Fourier undersampling) in a single two-phase recipe (corruption-aware pretraining + corruption-respecting distillation), subsuming several prior task-specific corruption-aware diffusion methods as special cases.

Novel conceptual contribution: the paper convincingly reframes score distillation not merely as an acceleration technique but as a quality-improving mechanism under corrupted-data training, backed by an intuitive mode-seeking argument (reverse vs. forward KL) as well as formal theory.

Strong and extensive empirical validation across many settings: denoising at multiple noise levels, Gaussian deblurring, random inpainting (multiple missing rates), super-resolution, and real multi-coil MRI reconstruction (FastMRI) at several acceleration factors, on CIFAR-10, FFHQ, CelebA-HQ, AFHQ-v2 and MRI data, consistently showing RSD improves over teacher diffusion models and often over few-shot baselines that use some clean images.

Non-trivial theoretical support: linear-Gaussian analysis (Theorem 1) with exact Wasserstein-2 bounds for global minimizers, extensions to general linear corruption operators and multiple noise scales (Theorems 2-4), a strict-saddle characterization of the loss landscape (Theorem 3), and more general nonparametric guarantees (Theorem 5, Corollary 1) connecting Fisher-divergence distillation loss to improvement over the noisy teacher — this is unusually rigorous support compared to typical empirical distillation papers.

Practical contributions beyond the core method: a "Proximal FID" model-selection criterion for settings without clean validation data (validated to track true FID closely across datasets/tasks), thorough ablations on distillation-loss choice, data scale, unknown/misspecified noise level, and demonstration of downstream usage as a prior for conditional inverse problems.

Efficiency gains are demonstrated concretely (wall-clock numbers for training and up to ~30x inference speedup), and reproducibility efforts are reasonable (detailed appendix algorithms/hyperparameters, promise to release code).
weaknesses: Datasets are relatively small-scale/low-resolution (CIFAR-10 32x32, FFHQ/CelebA-HQ/AFHQ-v2 64x64); it's unclear how the method scales to higher-resolution, more complex/diverse natural image distributions or larger foundation-scale diffusion models, which limits claims of broad significance.

Comparisons for some tasks (e.g., Gaussian deblurring, super-resolution, general operators) largely benchmark against the paper's own teacher models and a couple of few-shot baselines (EM-Diffusion); the set of competing baselines is somewhat narrow, and some baselines use partial clean data (50 images) while RSD uses none, making "surpassing" comparisons not fully apples-to-apples (though this is acknowledged).

The distillation stage relies on SiD's specific loss and default hyperparameters without task-specific tuning; the ablation explicitly notes SDS/DMD underperform partly due to lack of tuning, which somewhat weakens the generality claim that the framework is agnostic to distillation loss choice.

The theoretical results, while rigorous, rely on fairly strong simplifying assumptions (Gaussian/low-rank data, linear generator, perfect score estimation) that are quite far from the practical deep network setting; the general nonparametric bound (Theorem 5/Corollary 1) is more realistic but involves several abstract quantities (capacity/near-optimality assumptions, Poincaré-type constants) that are not empirically estimated or connected quantitatively to the experiments.

The paper is very dense with results spread across a large appendix (68 pages); some content (e.g., repeated qualitative figure grids) could be consolidated, and the core paper's main text stops short of stress-testing more complex/mixed corruption combinations or out-of-distribution operators at test time.

FastMRI experiments use a single teacher (Fourier-space Ambient Diffusion) and only FID as the generative-quality metric; more standard MRI reconstruction metrics (e.g., PSNR/SSIM against fully sampled ground truth, when available for a held-out subset) would strengthen the real-world medical-imaging claims.
